title: Undirected and directed graphs: two-way undirected edges vs. independent directed edges
summary: Contrast edge direction constraints on the same vertex layout using undirected segments and directed arrows.
context: Both the left and right figures contain five vertices numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in the exact same geometric layout (1 top-left, 3 bottom-left, 5 top-center, 2 bottom-center, 4 right) to contrast undirected and directed edges.
description: On the left is "Undirected graph (Edges have no direction)" with 7 arrowhead-free undirected edges: 1—2, 1—3, 1—5, 2—3, 2—4, 2—5, and 4—5. Every undirected edge inherently represents a two-way connection between two vertices; for example, edge 1—5 allows traversal both from 1 to 5 and from 5 to 1.

On the right is "Directed graph (Edges have a direction)" with 9 arrows, listed by tail vertex as 1→3, 2→1, 2→4, 2→5, 3→1, 3→2, 4→5, 5→1, and 5→4. Between vertices 1 and 3, and between 4 and 5, there is a pair of arrows in opposite directions, while the other five connections each have only a one-way arrow.

frames.title: Undirected and directed graphs: two-way undirected edges vs. independent directed edges
frames.explanation: Directed edges in opposite directions are independent of one another. For instance, the right graph has 5→1 without a direct 1→5, although 5 is still indirectly reachable from 1 via 1→3→2→5. Direct two-way reachability requires two opposite directed edges; an indirect path must not be mistaken for a direct edge.
